blocks.text: K. wondered whether he ought not to leave now with all haste; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect that he could do so during the sermon, he would then have to stay as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long ceased to be obliged to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was 11. But was there really to be a sermon? Could K. alone represent the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who merely wanted to look round the church? At bottom he was nothing else either. It was absurd to think that there was to be preaching, now at 11 o'clock, on a weekday, in the most abominable weather. The clergyman — a clergyman it undoubtedly was, a young man with a smooth, dark face — was evidently only going up to put out the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

But it was not so; rather, the clergyman examined the light and turned it up a little more, then he turned slowly towards the balustrade, which he grasped in front by its angular edging with both hands. So he stood for a while and, without moving his head, looked about him. K. had drawn back a good distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw somewhere, without determining the place precisely, the verger with his crooked back crouching down peacefully, as though after a completed task. What a stillness reigned now in the cathedral! But K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of staying here; if it was the clergyman's duty to preach at a fixed hour without regard to the circumstances, then let him do so, it would succeed without K.'s support as well, just as K.'s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. Slowly, then, K. set himself in motion, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then came out into the broad main aisle and walked there too quite undisturbed, except that the stone floor rang beneath the softest step and the vaults echoed it faintly but unceasingly, in manifold, regular progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked there alone between the empty pews, observed perhaps by the clergyman, and the size of the cathedral seemed to him to lie just at the limit of what was still bearable for human beings. When he came to his former place, he positively snatched, without further delay, at the album he had left lying there and took it with him. He had almost left the area of the pews and was approaching the open space that lay between them and the exit when he heard the clergyman's voice for the first time. A mighty, practised voice. How it pierced the cathedral that stood ready to receive it! But it was not the congregation that the clergyman was calling, it was quite unambiguous and there was no evading it, he called: Josef K.!

K. faltered and looked at the floor before him. For the moment he was still free, he could still walk on and make off through one of the three small dark wooden doors that were not far in front of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that he had understood but did not care to heed it. But if he turned round, he was held fast, for then he would have made the confession that he had understood perfectly well, that he really was the one called, and that he also meant to obey. Had the clergyman called once more, K. would certainly have gone away, but since everything remained still, however long K. waited, he did after all turn his head a little, for he wanted to see what the clergyman was doing now. He stood quietly in the pulpit as before, but it was plain to see that he had noticed K.'s turn of the head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned round completely. He did so and was summoned closer by the clergyman with a beckoning of the finger. Since everything could now take place openly, he ran — he did so also out of curiosity and in order to cut the matter short — with long flying strides towards the pulpit. At the first pews he halted, but the distance still seemed too great to the clergyman, he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered forefinger at a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. complied in this too; in this spot he already had to bend his head far back in order still to see the clergyman. “You are Josef K.,” said the clergyman, and raised one hand on the balustrade in a vague gesture. “Yes,” said K., he thought of how openly he had always given his name before, for some time now it had been a burden to him, and now people he was meeting for the first time knew his name too; how pleasant it had been to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You are accused,” said the clergyman, especially softly. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of it.” “Then you are the one I am looking for,” said the clergyman. “I am the prison chaplain.” “I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the clergyman, “in order to speak with you.” “I did not know that,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian the cathedral.” “Leave aside what is incidental,” said the clergyman. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” answered K., “it is an album of the town's sights.” “Put it down,” said the clergyman. K. flung it away so violently that it flew open and slid some way across the floor with crumpled pages. “Do you know that your trial is going badly?” asked the clergyman. “It seems so to me too,” said K. “I have taken every possible pains, but so far without success. Admittedly I have not yet finished the petition.” “How do you imagine the end,” asked the clergyman. “At first I thought it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you know?” “No,” said the clergyman, “but I fear it will end badly. You are held to be guilty. Your trial will perhaps never get beyond a lower court at all. At least for the present, your guilt is held to be proven.” “But I am not guilty,” said K. “It is a mistake. How can any man be guilty at all. We are all human beings here, after all, one like the other.” “That is true,” said the clergyman, “but that is how the guilty are wont to talk.” “Do you too have a prejudice against me?” asked K. “I have no prejudice against you,” said the clergyman. “I thank you,” said K. “But all the others who are involved in the proceedings have a prejudice against me. They instil it into those who are not involved as well. My position is growing ever more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the clergyman. “The verdict does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually pass over into the verdict.” “So that is how it is,” said K., and lowered his head. “What do you intend to do next in your case?” asked the clergyman. “I mean to seek further help,” said K., and raised his head to see what the clergyman thought of this. “There are still certain possibilities that I have not made use of.” “You seek too much help from others,” said the clergyman disapprovingly, “and especially from women. Do you not notice that it is not the true help.” “Sometimes, and even often, I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could move a few women I know to work together on my behalf, I would be bound to get through. Especially with this court, which consists almost entirely of woman-chasers. Show the examining magistrate a woman in the distance and, just to get there in time, he will run down the court table and the accused.” The clergyman inclined his head towards the balustrade; only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to press him down. What sort of storm could there be outside? This was no longer a dull day, this was already deep night. None of the stained glass in the great windows was able to break the dark wall with even a glimmer. And just now the verger began to put out the candles on the high altar, one after another. “Are you angry with me,” K. asked the clergyman. “Perhaps you do not know what kind of court you serve.” He received no answer. “These are only my own experiences, after all,” said K. Above, all remained silent still. “I did not mean to offend you,” said K. Then the clergyman shrieked down at K.: “Can you not see two steps in front of you?” It was shouted in anger, but at the same time as by one who sees someone fall and, because he himself is startled, cries out unguardedly, without meaning to.
